questions.question: Explain how a child inherits features from both parents and why brothers and sisters are not identical. Name four inherited human features.
questions.expected_answer: Genes are carried on chromosomes in the nucleus; humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs, one of each pair from each parent. Each sex cell (egg or sperm) carries a random selection of one chromosome from each pair, so when a sperm fertilises an egg the child receives a unique combination; siblings receive different combinations and so differ. Inherited features: height (with environmental effects), natural eye colour, natural hair type, blood group, tongue rolling, earlobe shape, dimples.

questions.question: Describe how you would plan a fair survey of height in your class, including two ethical considerations.
questions.expected_answer: Ask a clear question, such as how height varies in the class. Measure everyone the same way: shoes off, back and heels against a wall, looking ahead, a flat object on the head, read at eye level to the nearest half centimetre, using the same tape; repeat and average if needed. Survey as many learners as possible. Record in a table with headings and units (cm). Ethics: get everyone's agreement to take part; use numbers or codes instead of names; do not use results to tease or embarrass anyone; treat sensitive data privately.

questions.question: In a class of 30, heights ranged from 138 cm to 165 cm and 21 learners could roll their tongues. Calculate the range and the percentage of tongue rollers, and state which graph you would use for each feature and why.
questions.expected_answer: Range = 165 - 138 = 27 cm. Tongue rollers: 21 ÷ 30 = 0,7 = 70 per cent. Height is continuous variation, so group it into equal intervals and draw a histogram with touching bars, because heights can take any value. Tongue rolling is discontinuous (two separate groups), so draw a bar graph with separate bars and gaps, or a pie chart.
